extracted.intended_audience: bankruptcy lawyers, judges, legal scholars, and practitioners involved in Chapter 11 mass-tort reorganizations
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a Chapter 11 reorganization plan may appropriately include releases of claims against non-debtors under 11 U.S.C. §1123(b)(6), using established doctrinal factors and contextual considerations (mass-tort context, preservation/enhancement of the estate, creditor approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness under §1123(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The key statutory term in §1123(b)(6) is “appropriate.” The term is broad and context dependent and confers broad discretion on a bankruptcy court to exercise reasonable discretion in Chapter 11 reorganization plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a provision is “appropriate” requires a holistic, context‑dependent inquiry; the language is open‑ended and includes consideration of all relevant factors, requiring flexibility and judgment (citing cases such as Michigan v. EPA; School Comm. of Burlington; Tanzin v. Tanvir).

rubrics_metrics.name: Released party closely related to the debtor
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the released party is closely related to the debtor (for example, through an indemnification agreement) where a suit against the non‑debtor is, in essence, a suit against the debtor or will deplete the assets of the estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close relation can include ownership, control, indemnification obligations, or other connections that make suits against the non‑debtor equivalent to suits against the debtor (quotation: “a suit against the non‑debtor is, in essence, a suit against the debtor or will deplete the assets of the estate”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are factually and legally intertwined
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claims against the non‑debtor are factually and legally intertwined with claims against the debtor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intertwining means the non‑debtor claims are deeply connected to, or essentially identical with, the debtor’s claims so that separate litigation would threaten the estate or undermine the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of releases must be tailored
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the scope of the releases is tailored to only the claims that must be released to protect the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases should be narrowly tailored—limited to claims that directly affect the res of the debtor’s estates (e.g., claims that would trigger indemnification or contribution rights)—and should not be broader than necessary to solve the collective‑action problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release is essential to the plan’s success
rubrics_metrics.description: Approve a release only if it is truly “essential” to the plan’s success and the reorganization would fail without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor ensures releases are used only where necessary to preserve or create the estate and to achieve fair and equitable recovery otherwise unattainable; courts should require a showing that without the release the plan could not succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-debtor paid substantial assets into the estate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether, as part of the settlement, the non‑debtor party has paid “substantial assets” to the estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents releases from being a free ride for non‑debtors; substantial payments demonstrate that the release is supported by meaningful consideration that enlarges the pool available to creditors and victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan provides fair payment to creditors for released claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the plan provides “fair payment” to creditors for their released claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors five and six together assess fairness of the settlement given the probability and likely amount of recovery from the non‑debtor; courts should evaluate whether creditors receive fair compensation relative to those prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overwhelming creditor and victim approval (supermajority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether creditors and victims overwhelmingly approve the release; the Second Circuit has defined a 75 percent approval as a bare minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High levels of creditor/victim approval (often well above 75% in mass‑tort cases) tend to show the plan is acceptable and that the release is solving a holdout problem; some courts require even higher supermajorities for non‑debtor releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-debtor releases confined to narrow circumstances addressing collective‑action problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑debtor releases are appropriate only in narrow and relatively rare circumstances—precisely those where collective‑action problems threaten fair and equitable recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice and judicially developed factors confine non‑debtor releases to cases where they solve coordination problems (e.g., mass‑tort bankruptcies) by preventing piecemeal litigation that would deplete estate assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Releases appropriate when they preserve and increase the estate
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑debtor releases are especially appropriate when the release and corresponding settlement payments preserve and increase the debtor’s estate and thereby ensure fair and equitable recovery for creditors and victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical demonstration (e.g., non‑debtor payments that 'enlarge the pie') and historical examples (Johns‑Manville, A. H. Robins, Dow Corning, Boy Scouts, dioceses) support this criterion; courts should consider whether the settlement meaningfully augments distributable assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensual confirmation thresholds for plans
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan is 'said to be confirmed consensually' if every class supporting the plan has a majority in number and at least two‑thirds in amount, even if some classes have dissenting creditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While consensual confirmation applies to debtor releases, courts have demanded even higher levels of support for non‑debtor releases in many appellate decisions; non‑consensual releases impose additional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy provides unique tools (binding all claimants) and reduces administrative costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Bankruptcy is the appropriate forum for coordinating mass‑tort claims because it binds all creditors, reduces administrative costs, pauses litigation, and allows collective resolution considering current and future victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contextual criterion supports using non‑debtor releases: the availability of binding, centralized distribution and procedural safeguards (e.g., discovery) are part of the justification for releases in mass‑tort cases; multi‑district litigation and class settlements cannot reliably achieve the same binding, equitable distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-debtor release tailoring to indemnification relationships and insurance assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should address specific mechanisms by which non‑debtor suits would deplete the estate—e.g., indemnification agreements or direct actions against insurers that would divert insurance proceeds from the bankruptcy estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court should evaluate indemnification terms, insurance coverage, and whether litigation against non‑debtors/insurers would consume shared assets, thereby justifying targeted releases to preserve estate resources.
